Title: Invalid Free of Stack Buffer in Lightweight ASN.1 X.509 Certificate Parser
Analysis:
In `lib/vtls/x509asn1.c`, the function `utf8asn1str` converts decoded wide characters (from Universal or BMP ASN.1 strings) to UTF-8. Within this function, `buf` is a stack-allocated buffer (`char buf[4];` at line 374). If a wide character `wc` parsed from an untrusted certificate is greater than or equal to `0x00200000` (which is an invalid value for target encoding), the code attempts to free `buf` via `free(buf);` at line 393. Since `buf` is allocated on the stack rather than the heap, calling `free()` on it causes an invalid free, memory corruption, and undefined behavior, which can be leveraged for code execution or a Denial of Service (DoS) attack. The vulnerability is reachable during the TLS handshake for any curl connection configured with a backend that makes use of the lightweight ASN.1 parser (e.g. WolfSSL, GnuTLS, Schannel, Secure Transport) when certificate info gathering is enabled.

**Conceptual Exploit Payload**:
A malicious server during the TLS handshake serves a specially crafted X.509 certificate. The certificate has a Subject Common Name (CN) encoded as a `UniversalString` containing a wide character with a value of `0x00200000` or higher.
When curl connects with a vulnerable TLS backend and parses the certificate, `Curl_extract_certinfo` invokes `utf8asn1str` to decode the CN. When the parser encounters the wide character, it triggers the `wc >= 0x00200000` condition and calls `free(buf)`, resulting in a crash or corruption of the stack frame.

Title: Out of Bounds Read in Lightweight ASN.1 OID Parser
Analysis:
In `lib/vtls/x509asn1.c`, the function `encodeOID` parses the dotted segment of an Object Identifier (OID) from an ASN.1 element inside an X.509 certificate. A sub-identifier in a DER/ASN.1 OID is represented by a sequence of bytes where the most significant bit (MSB, `0x80`) of each byte is set, except for the last byte of the sub-identifier which has the MSB cleared. In `encodeOID`, when parsing trailing numbers inside the `do-while` loop, the variable `beg` is incremented after reading each byte via `y = *(const unsigned char *) beg++;`. However, there is no boundary check (i.e. `beg < end`) inside this nested `do-while` loop. If the last byte of the parsed OID element has its MSB set (which is invalid for a DER OID, but possible in a malformed certificate), the `do-while` loop will continue to execute. On the next iteration, it reads past the `end` boundary of the OID buffer. Since there are no checks, the loop will read out of bounds from adjacent heap/stack memory until it happens to find a byte with the MSB cleared (or it crashes). This can be triggered by a malicious certificate during a TLS handshake, leading to an application crash (Denial of Service) or information disclosure.

**Conceptual Exploit Payload**:
A malicious server supplies an X.509 certificate during the TLS handshake. The certificate contains a signature algorithm or other OID field where the very last byte of the OID data has the MSB set (e.g. `0x80`). When curl connects and processes the certificate, `encodeOID` parses this OID. It enters the `do-while` loop, processes the byte, sees that `y & 0x80` is true, and then on the next iteration does `y = *(const unsigned char *) beg++;` where `beg` is equal to `end`. This reads beyond the boundaries of the parsed OID buffer, leading to an out-of-bounds read of adjacent heap memory.
